prompt: After `javac -d out Greet.java`, where is `Greet.class`?
hint: `-d` names a directory.

choices.text: Beside `Greet.java`, as in lesson 1
choices.why: That is where it goes without `-d`; with it, the source directory kept only the source.

choices.text: In `out`, a directory `javac` created for it
choices.why: Right: `javac` created `out` because it did not exist and wrote the class there.

choices.text: Nowhere on disk until `java` asks for it
choices.why: That describes source-file mode, `java Greet.java`; `javac` always writes a file.

choices.text: In `~/.cache`, where the JDK keeps compiled classes
choices.why: The JDK keeps no such cache; the class went exactly where `-d` said.

prompt: `java -cp out Greet Ana Bruno` runs. What is `args.length` inside `main`?
hint: Count only what comes after the class name.

choices.text: 4, one for each word after `java`
choices.why: `-cp`, `out` and `Greet` are for `java` itself; the program never sees them.

choices.text: 3, the class name and the two names
choices.why: The class name is not passed to the program, unlike `argv[0]` in C.
Right: `Ana` and `Bruno`, and the program printed two lines.

prompt: `java -cp out Greet` with no names: what number did `echo $?` print?
hint: The number passed to `System.exit`.

prompt: Why does `Greet` print its usage line with `System.err` rather than `System.out`?
hint: Think of `java -cp out Greet > names.txt`.

choices.text: So a redirect of the output does not swallow the message
choices.why: Right: `>` captures standard output only, and the complaint still reaches the screen.

choices.text: Because only `System.err` can be followed by `System.exit`
choices.why: `System.exit` can follow anything; the stream and the status are unrelated.

choices.text: Because `System.err` prints in red, which marks an error
choices.why: Nothing in the transcript is coloured; the difference is where the text goes.

choices.text: Because the shell sets `$?` from what is written to `System.err`
choices.why: `$?` comes from `System.exit`, or from `main` returning, never from the text.

prompt: `java -cp out Greet.class` fails with `ClassNotFoundException: Greet.class`. What did `java` look for?
hint: `java` reads a class name, and a dot means something in one.

choices.text: A file called `Greet.class.class` in `out`
choices.why: Close in spirit, but the dot changes the meaning: it separates a package from a class.

choices.text: A class called `class` in a package called `Greet`
choices.why: Right: the dot is a package separator, which is why the fix is dropping the extension.

choices.text: The file `Greet.class` in the current directory, ignoring `-cp`
choices.why: `-cp out` was honoured; the class path was right and the name was wrong.

choices.text: A source file `Greet.class` to compile in memory
choices.why: Source-file mode starts only for a name ending in `.java`, or with `--source`.

prompt: Which of these commands fail with `Could not find or load main class`, run in `~/life` where the class is in `out`? Choose all that apply.
hint: The name must be exact, and the place must be on the class path.

choices.text: `java Greet Ana`
choices.why: Yes: with no `-cp` the class path is the current directory, and the class is not there.

choices.text: `java -cp out greet Ana`
choices.why: Yes: class names are case-sensitive.

choices.text: `java -cp out Greet`
choices.why: No: it finds the class and runs it; it prints the usage line and exits with 2, which is the program working.

choices.text: `java Greet.java Ana`
choices.why: No: the source file is right there, and source-file mode compiles and runs it.

prompt: What does `java Greet.java Ana` leave on disk?
hint: `ls` was run right after.

choices.text: `Greet.class`, beside the source
choices.why: That is what `javac` does; `ls` showed only `Greet.java`.

choices.text: A cached class under `~/.java`, reused next time
choices.why: There is no such cache: the class lived in the JVM's memory and every run compiles again.

choices.text: Nothing new: the class lived in memory
choices.why: Right: it compiled in memory, ran, and wrote nothing.

prompt: `time` measured 1.093 s for `java Greet.java Ana` and 0.206 s for `java Greet Ana` from a compiled class. Roughly how many times longer did the source run take? Give a whole number.
hint: Divide the first by the second.

prompt: `Main.java` uses `Shout`, which is in `Shout.java` beside it. On Java 25, what does `java Main.java` do?
hint: Java 22 changed the answer.

choices.text: Fails, because source-file mode compiles one file only
choices.why: That was true up to 21; since 22 it compiles the other classes it needs from the same directory.

choices.text: Compiles both in memory and runs `Main`
choices.why: Right: it found `Shout.java` by the class name and printed `HELLO FROM TWO FILES!`.

choices.text: Compiles every `.java` file in the directory, then runs `Main`
choices.why: Only what is needed: a broken `Broken.java` beside them was never looked at.

choices.text: Asks which file holds `main`, because both are public classes
choices.why: The file you name is the one whose `main` runs; nothing is asked.

prompt: You copy the script `greet`, `#!` line and all, to `greet.java` and run `java greet.java Ana`. Why does it fail?
hint: What does `--source 25` do for a file without an extension?

choices.text: A script cannot be run by naming it after `java`
choices.why: A script can; the extension is what changed, not the way it was started.

choices.text: A `.java` file is compiled as plain Java, where `#` is an illegal character
choices.why: Right: the compiler stopped at line 1, and only an extensionless file run with `--source` has its `#!` line skipped.

choices.text: The file is not executable after `cp`
choices.why: `java greet.java` reads the file; it does not need the execute bit.

prompt: Match what you have to the command that runs it.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

pairs.left: An executable file with a `#!` line

prompt: Which JDK tool lists the JVMs running under your user, with their process ids?
hint: Its name is the shell's `ps` with a `j`.

choices.text: `jps`
choices.why: Right: and `-l` adds the main class.

choices.text: `jcmd`
choices.why: `jcmd` sends a command to one JVM; `jps` is the one that lists them.

choices.text: `javap`
choices.why: `javap` reads class files on disk, not running processes.

choices.text: `jshell`
choices.why: `jshell` runs Java line by line; it lists nothing.

prompt: `Wait` starts no threads, and `jcmd Wait Thread.print` counted 18. Where do the other 17 come from?
hint: Whose process is it?

choices.text: From `Thread.sleep`, which starts a thread per second it waits
choices.why: `sleep` pauses the thread that calls it; it starts nothing.

choices.text: From `jcmd`, which copies its own threads into the target
choices.why: One thread answered `jcmd`, and it belongs to the target JVM; `jcmd` copies nothing.

choices.text: From the JVM itself: the garbage collector, the JIT compilers and others
choices.why: Right: the process is the JVM, and `main` is one thread among its own.

choices.text: From other Java programs of yours, which share one JVM
choices.why: Each `java` command is a process of its own; `jps` lists them separately.

prompt: To ask a running JVM which JDK it is running on, you type `jcmd Wait ___`.
hint: Two words joined by a dot.

prompt: `-Xlog:class+load` printed 605 lines for `Greet`, and 600 came from the shared objects file. What does that archive buy?
hint: It was prepared before the program existed.

choices.text: A smaller program: classes in it are not counted in memory
choices.why: They are in memory all the same; what changes is how they got there.

choices.text: A faster start: library classes arrive already parsed and checked, mapped rather than loaded one by one
choices.why: Right: that is the `sharing` in `java -version`'s last line.

choices.text: Your own classes compiled to machine code in advance
choices.why: Your `Greet` came from `out`; the archive holds the JDK's library.

prompt: `ps` reported 44,080 KB for `java Wait`, a program that holds one string. Where does most of that memory go?
hint: Count what is in the process besides your code.

choices.text: To the string, which Java stores with large padding
choices.why: A short string is a few dozen bytes; it is nowhere near the total.

choices.text: To the 60,000 milliseconds `sleep` reserves
choices.why: Sleeping reserves no memory; it is a pause.

choices.text: To the JVM itself and the library classes it loaded
choices.why: Right: the JVM, its threads and hundreds of classes are the bulk of it.

prompt: A script runs `java -cp app/classes Report` and then decides from `$?` whether to e-mail the result. `Report` ends with an exception it never catches. What does the script see?
hint: An exception escaping `main` has its own status.

choices.text: 0, because the JVM itself ended normally
choices.why: An escaping exception is a failure, and the JVM reports it.

choices.text: 1, the status of an exception escaping `main`
choices.why: Right: 0 when `main` returns, 1 when an exception escapes it, or whatever `System.exit` was given.

choices.text: 127, because the class could not finish loading
choices.why: 127 is the shell's code for a command that does not exist; `java` did exist.

choices.text: 2, the status used for usage errors
choices.why: 2 is what `Greet` chose for itself; nothing makes it a default.

prompt: Put the steps of `java -cp out Greet Ana` in order.
hint: The process exists before any of your code.
items: The operating system starts the JVM process
The JVM finds `Greet.class` in `out` and loads it

prompt: A colleague's service on a shared server misbehaves, and three JDKs are installed there. Which single command tells you which one that running service is using?
hint: Ask the process, not the machine.

choices.text: `java -version`
choices.why: That reports the `java` your shell would start now, which may not be the one that started the service.

choices.text: `update-alternatives --display java`
choices.why: That says where `/usr/bin/java` points; the service may have been started by a full path.

choices.text: `jcmd <pid> VM.version`, with the service's process id
choices.why: Right: the running JVM answers for itself, whatever started it.

choices.text: `ls /usr/lib/jvm`
choices.why: That lists the three JDKs; it does not say which one is running.

prompt: Which way of running a program writes no `.class` file to disk?
hint: One of them compiles in memory.

choices.text: `javac -d out Greet.java` and then `java -cp out Greet`
choices.why: `javac` wrote `out/Greet.class`.

choices.text: `java Greet.java`
choices.why: Right: the source-file mode compiles in memory and keeps nothing.

choices.text: `javac Greet.java` and then `java Greet`
choices.why: That writes `Greet.class` beside the source, as lesson 1 did.
